sections.title: Reading Comprehension · Passage B
sections.intro: Read “This Life” and answer questions 10–14. A vocabulary note follows the poem.

passage.title: This Life
passage.credit: —Rita Dove · from The Poets Laureate Anthology (2010), W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.

lines.text: My grandmother told me there’d be good days
to counter the dark ones,
with blue skies in the heart as far
as the soul could see. She said
you could measure a life in as many ways
as there were to bake a pound cake,
but you still needed real butter and eggs
for a good one—pound cake, that is,
but I knew what she meant. She was always
talking around corners like that;
she knew words carried their treasures
like a grape clusters around its own juice.
She loved words; she thought a book
was a monument to the glory of creation
and a library … well, sometimes
just trying to describe Jubilation
will get you a bit tongue, so let’s
leave it at that. But my grandmother
was nobody’s fool, and she’d tell anybody
smart enough to listen. Don’t let a little pain
stop you; try as hard as you can
every minute you’re given or else
sit down and shut-up—though in her opinion,
keeping quiet in noisy times was a sin
against everything God and democracy
intended us for. I know she’d like
where I’m standing right now. She’d say
a man who could measure his life in deeds
was larger inside than the vessel that carried him;
she’d say he was a cluster of grapes.
My grandmother was only four feet ten
but when she entered a room, even the books
came to attention. Giants come in all sizes:
Sometimes a moment is a monument;
sometimes an institution breathes—
like a library. Like this halcyon¹ day.
¹ halcyon — peaceful

questions.explanation: The grandmother says good days will counter dark ones and imagines blue skies within the heart. She expects hope even during difficulty, showing optimism.

questions.prompt: The figurative language in lines 9 and 10 highlights the grandmother’s
questions.explanation: The narrator says the grandmother talked “around corners,” using the pound-cake comparison to communicate a broader lesson indirectly. Figurative language was her way of teaching wisdom.

questions.prompt: Which phrase from the poem clarifies the narrator’s statement in line 30?
questions.explanation: The “cluster of grapes” metaphor evokes a person rich in meaningful accomplishments. The nearby phrase “measure his life in deeds” explains what that inner abundance means.

questions.prompt: The personification in lines 32 and 33 emphasizes the grandmother’s
questions.explanation: The books seem to stand at attention when the short grandmother enters. Giving books a human response emphasizes how commanding her presence is despite her physical size.

questions.prompt: The overall tone of the poem can best be described as
questions.explanation: The speaker remembers the grandmother’s optimism, wisdom, and powerful presence with affection and admiration. That produces a respectful tone.
